an1.1:2.1: Technically, it is not the sight that “occupies” the mind (literally “having invaded, remains”), but the unskillful qualities provoked by the sight ([an8.63:1.7]()). Hence this does not occur for one free of desire ([an6.55:17.1]()). As to what might have prompted such a strong statement, at [an5.55]() a similar passage is spoken in response to a mother and son, who, while ordained as monk and nun, had sex with each other. Elsewhere, it is said that possessions, honor, and popularity have an even more powerful effect on the mind ([sn17.21](), [sn17.22]()).
an1.1:2.2: This chapter of discourses gives the impression of being a single longer discourse split into two sets of five so as to fill out the Book of the Ones. In fact, while it is rarely possible to prove such changes, it seems that many of the discourses in the Ones (and the Twos) have been produced this way (but see [an1.58]() and note there). What we have in the text today are fragments of longer, more coherent teachings.
an1.6:1.1: As to why the Book of the Ones begins with such a strong statement on the dangers of sexual attraction, I believe the book as a whole was compiled as a beginner text for young monastics, perhaps around the time of the Second Council, 100 years after the Buddha (see note for Bakkula at [an1.226:1.1]()).
